headline: The biggest manipulation gains today come from evolving the harness around a frozen model, while the papers that matter most for human-facing robots show policies that start moving when nobody asked, pick the wrong object in clutter, and change how people feel in ways that physical metrics miss.
thesis: Several groups now improve robots without touching policy weights: a coding model rewrites the control harness, a teacher's harness is distilled into a 4B student, or lessons from past runs are stored as context. That makes the evaluation harness part of the product, and today's evaluation papers show how often cheap proxies (offline loss, a clean build, a module's name, a VLM judge) disagree with what actually runs. The behaviours those proxies miss are the ones people notice first: every tested VLA checkpoint moved on an empty instruction, generalists acted on the wrong object 30% of the time in clutter, and dual-encoder VLMs scored at chance on single-attribute changes. On the human side, an exosuit study and a dog-navigation pilot both show that what a robot does physically does not predict how it is perceived, so perception and choices have to be measured directly. Human data keeps getting cheaper to use, since action-free video, contact geometry and object motion carry most of the transfer, and humanoid motion generators are being closed around robot feedback so they can respond to people mid-motion.

clusters.title: Agent harnesses around frozen models are now evolved automatically, and they carry most of the gain
clusters.why: Improving a robot on a new setup has usually meant fine-tuning the policy. RoboArchitect has a coding model revise the harness around a frozen policy and raises unseen-scene success from 9.7% to 43.3% (2610.42141), TinyAstral accepts harness edits only after a paired statistical test and then distills a 4B student that scores 62.8% against its teacher's 63.6% (2610.41216), LEXP keeps weights fixed and stores lessons with applicability conditions (2610.41320), SketchMate stores a geometric sketch per task and reuses it in 3.4 s instead of about 90 s (2610.41844), and REA routes between a slow brain and fast policies using a memory of measured policy success (2610.42053). Before fine-tuning for a new site, iterate on tools, recovery logic and memory in the wrapper, and version that wrapper like any other component.

clusters.title: Policies act when they should hold still or choose another object, so benchmark success overstates readiness for human spaces
clusters.why: Benchmarks mostly measure whether a policy completes the instructed task in a tidy scene. With an empty or nonsense instruction, all six VLA checkpoints tested started moving and five often finished a task nobody asked for (2610.41609). In clutter, zero-shot generalists acted on the wrong object 30% of the time (2610.41377), and RL post-training made a person-following VLA more persistent but raised collisions with distractors until an execution-time risk gate stepped in (2610.41275). Underneath, 22 dual-encoder VLMs scored at or below chance when only one attribute or relation changed (2610.41118), and adding depth made VLM spatial reasoning worse in mirror scenes (2610.41651). Treat 'do nothing', 'which one' and look-alike distractors as their own test cases, and make the decision to start moving an explicit gate rather than a prompt instruction.

clusters.title: Cheap proxies (offline metrics, a clean build, a module's name) keep disagreeing with what actually runs
clusters.why: Teams pick checkpoints by validation loss, accept code that compiles, and trust a component because of what it is called. Across 281 real-robot policies, only five of 67 offline metrics tracked insertion success, and only within one policy family (2610.40828). 56.5% of LLM-generated ROS1-to-ROS2 migrations built and then failed at runtime (2610.41168), two world-model harness revisions moved accuracy by 0.2 and 2.6 points while changing 11 and 214 test verdicts (2610.41130), and in an audited agent 18 of 25 named cognitive modules never reached any output (2610.41604). Keep real-robot or launch-level tests in the loop, compare versions test by test rather than by aggregate score, and check that each named component actually changes behaviour.

clusters.title: Physical metrics do not predict how people, or animals, experience a robot
clusters.why: Assistive and HRI work often uses a physical outcome (lower muscle load, a path designed to be legible) to stand in for experience. With an elbow exosuit, assistance reduced muscle activity, yet perceived weight, adaptation and effort-based choices followed participants' initial experience rather than the biomechanical change (2610.41679). A curve-out pass designed from legible-motion theory caused a more acute stress response in a dog than a straight pass, which the authors attribute to the robot stopping and reorienting to approximate the arc (2610.40921). An essay on architectural robots argues that their effects persist in the configuration left behind and can favour some occupants over others (2610.41724). Measure perception, adaptation and decisions directly, record each participant's first exposure, and check that a legible plan is executed smoothly enough to read as one motion.

clusters.title: Action labels are the scarce part: video, contacts and object motion carry most of the transfer
clusters.why: Robot learning has treated action-labelled teleoperation as the necessary currency. WorldBridge raises out-of-distribution success from 25.07% to 55.90% by adding action-free videos of the new tasks, and to 70.70% with one labelled demonstration per task (2610.40748). CIMI aligns contact surfaces before retargeting and gains at least 50 points over baselines across six hand-task pairs (2610.41028), HandMimicX defines the RL objective on object motion rather than the hand path (2610.41336), Nexus-VLA trains on human and robot data jointly through a shared semantic latent (2610.42021), and MotorSense pairs 100 hours of egocentric video with EMG (2610.41127). When planning data collection, task breadth and contact information appear to buy more than dense per-task action labels.

clusters.title: Humanoid motion generators are being closed around robot feedback and steered at run time instead of tracking a fixed reference
clusters.why: The common humanoid pipeline generates a reference motion and hands it to an independent tracker, so drift and disturbances never reach the generator. HIPC feeds realized states back to a goal-conditioned motion planner and handles the resulting distribution shift with deviation-decayed recovery and history re-anchoring (2610.41334). DiffWBC makes the whole-body controller a one-step diffusion model that cost gradients can steer at test time (0.84 clean pass under a 1.25 m ceiling versus 0.10 for reference editing) and that flags its own likely failures (2610.41354). Movens-Zero chunks motion under continuously updated text, speech, music or video conditions (2610.41877). A social humanoid that gestures while people talk and move around it needs a generator that sees its own state and accepts new conditions mid-motion.

insights: Add a 'no task' suite before putting a VLA near people. In 2610.41609 every tested checkpoint started moving on an empty instruction, and a prompt prefix telling it not to move stopped none of them, while a gate comparing the first action chunk against the empty-instruction chunk held the robot in five of six checkpoints. Speech recognition errors, small talk and half-finished sentences all reach a human-facing robot as non-task text, so log what your stack does on them and implement the start-of-motion decision as an explicit node (for example a ROS 2 action server precondition) rather than relying on the policy.

Measure what people perceive and decide, not only what the robot does to their body. The exosuit study (2610.41679) found perceived weight and effort-based choices were shaped by participants' initial experience, and the dog pilot (2610.40921) found a 'legible' manoeuvre became a stressor when executed with stops. In user studies, counterbalance condition order, record first exposure as a covariate, and replay the executed trajectory (not the planned one) when judging legibility.

Try iterating on the harness before fine-tuning, but audit it. RoboArchitect (2610.42141) and TinyAstral (2610.41216) get large gains without changing policy weights, and TinyAstral only accepts an edit after a paired statistical test. The module audit (2610.41604) is the counterweight: 18 of 25 named modules never reached any output. If you add memory, lessons or 'theory of mind' components to a social robot, check with a simple ablation that each one changes behaviour, and version the harness together with the model.

Do not pick dexterous policies offline. In 2610.40828, observation and action representation (cropping to a region of interest, robot-base frame, absolute rather than relative actions) moved success by tens of points while optimizer choices did not, and offline metrics only shortlisted. Fix representation choices first, then spend real-robot trials on the shortlist. The same lesson applies to LLM-assisted ROS 2 migration: in 2610.41168 most failures compiled cleanly, so require launch tests that exercise topics, services and actions.

must_read.why: A robot that moves when nobody asked is a direct safety and trust problem around people, and this is the first systematic test of it on current VLAs.
must_read.key_idea: Hold the initial state fixed, vary only the instruction (empty, neutral, nonsense, infeasible, wrong task), and ask whether the robot starts moving, which task it completes, and what the instruction actually determines.
must_read.evidence: Six checkpoints in LIBERO-Goal simulation; with an empty instruction the robot started moving in every episode for all six, and five often completed an unrequested task; a 'do not move' prompt prefix stopped none, a first-chunk similarity gate held the robot on non-task inputs in five of six, and fine-tuning prevented task completion but did not reliably keep the robot still.
must_read.caveat: Simulation only, in one benchmark suite; instructions are typed text rather than real speech, and no real robot or human study is reported.

must_read.why: It shows directly, with human participants, that physical assistance metrics do not predict perception or decisions, which is the assumption behind most assistive-robot evaluations.
must_read.key_idea: Evaluate force augmentation on weight perception, adaptation to a changing environment and effort-based decision-making alongside muscle activity, and test whether the cognitive outcomes follow the biomechanical one.
must_read.evidence: Elbow-assisting exosuit during lifting; assistance reduced muscle activity and perceived weight, but the weight effect depended strongly on initial experience, adaptation to changing contingencies was selectively reduced, and effort-based decisions followed initial experience rather than reductions in muscle activity or perceived fatigue.
must_read.caveat: The abstract gives no participant count or demographics, and it covers one device and one lifting task; extending the finding to non-wearable robots is our inference.

must_read.why: One of the largest real-robot ablations of imitation learning, and it tells you which design choices are worth your limited robot time.
must_read.key_idea: Run controlled ablations across many policy families on one hard real task, and test whether any offline metric can stand in for real-robot success.
must_read.evidence: 281 policies from seven families in about 1,700 real trials of RJ45 grasping and insertion with a five-fingered hand; ROI cropping, base-frame representation and in-encoder normalization each improved point-cloud policies by 70-100 points, and absolute actions improved VLA insertion by up to 70 points; only five of 67 offline metrics correlated with success (r = -0.70 to -0.80), and only within one family.
must_read.caveat: A single insertion task on one hand; skill decomposition, multi-view perception and recovery demonstrations were associated with the best systems but not independently isolated.

must_read.why: It gives the clearest numbers today for how much a frozen policy can gain from an automatically revised harness, without any retraining.
must_read.key_idea: A coding model watches rollouts, diagnoses failures and rewrites the control code around a frozen policy (when to call it, when to use vision tools, when to command the arm directly), including a persistent memory it designs itself.
must_read.evidence: Average success on held-out scenes rose from 9.7% to 43.3% and on held-out tasks from 12.7% to 40.2% across multiple benchmarks and policies; learned strategies include lifting a jammed arm clear and reaching in horizontally around obstacles.
must_read.caveat: The abstract does not say whether evaluation is in simulation or on real hardware, or name the benchmarks; each new setup still needs rollouts to evolve its harness.

must_read.why: Its tasks are grounded in developmental cognitive science and target the clutter, occlusion and 'which part do I grab' reasoning that home and care robots face.
must_read.key_idea: Turn a developmental taxonomy of reasoning (occlusion, containment, support, affordances, hidden objects) into executable manipulation tasks, so policies must both recognize the structure and act correctly in it.
must_read.evidence: Zero-shot generalist policies drop by over 50% in success as distractors increase, act on the wrong object 30% of the time in clutter, and select the correct object part only about 50% of the time even with specific prompts; VLM-based success estimation was also unreliable on these rollouts.
must_read.caveat: Simulation only and zero-shot policies only; fine-tuned or harness-wrapped policies were not tested, so the gap for a deployed system is not measured.

2610.42141.problem: Agent harnesses that make frozen policies useful are hand-built for each robot and benchmark.
2610.42141.method: A coding model watches rollouts, diagnoses failures and revises the harness code and its persistent memory around a frozen policy.
2610.42141.why: Without weight updates, unseen-scene success rose from 9.7% to 43.3%, an alternative to fine-tuning on a new setup.

2610.41216.problem: Harness improvements found with large planners are expensive to run on robot-side compute.
2610.41216.method: Evolve a frozen teacher's harness with edits accepted only after a paired statistical test, then distill a 4B student that runs in the same harness.
2610.41216.why: The 4B student reaches 62.8% on RoboTwin against the teacher's 63.6% using about one fifth of its accelerator time.

2610.41320.problem: Multimodal reasoners can manipulate but do not improve from their own execution experience.
2610.41320.method: Keeps weights fixed and stores lessons with applicability conditions extracted from execution evidence, reused as feedback for later actions.
2610.41320.why: 23/36 real trials against 2/36 for the vanilla model, a lightweight way for a deployed robot to accumulate site-specific know-how.

2610.41844.problem: VLM-based zero-shot manipulation is far too coarse for keyed sub-millimetre insertion.
2610.41844.method: A VLM agent builds a sketch of geometric primitives and mate frames using depth tools, stores it, and reuses it by point-cloud registration.
2610.41844.why: 88% insertion on 69 simulated episodes where ReKep and MOKA insert none, and reuse cuts sketch time from about 90 s to 3.4 s.

2610.42053.problem: Pairing slow foundation-model reasoning with fast policies either stalls execution or misses silent failures.
2610.42053.method: A runtime where no running policy waits on the brain, using a route memory of measured policy success, a boundary-triggered judge and a bounded escalation ladder.
2610.42053.why: 95.9% on LIBERO-Pro with 25% fewer control steps, and it transfers to a real Unitree G1.

2610.41609.problem: VLA policies are tested on completing instructed tasks, not on staying still when there is no instruction.
2610.41609.method: Paired tests with empty, neutral, nonsense, infeasible and wrong-task instructions on six checkpoints, followed by three start-suppression methods.
2610.41609.why: Every checkpoint moved on an empty instruction; robots near people who talk without commanding need a start gate, and a prompt prefix does not work.

2610.41377.problem: Simulation benchmarks test low-level execution in clean scenes and miss commonsense reasoning about occlusion, containment and affordances.
2610.41377.method: A taxonomy grounded in developmental cognitive science turned into tasks on hidden objects, support relations and semantically correct grasp points.
2610.41377.why: Zero-shot generalists act on the wrong object 30% of the time in clutter, so current benchmarks likely overstate readiness for homes.

2610.41275.problem: RL post-training of a person-following VLA improves persistence but raises collisions with look-alike distractors.
2610.41275.method: A calibrated execution-time risk gate that rescales only the translational part of the next waypoint when target-state risk is high.
2610.41275.why: Cuts distracted-tracking collisions by 3.96 points while matching the policy's action on over 98% of steps.

2610.41118.problem: Image-text compositionality benchmarks pair images that differ in most pixels, so scores are confounded.
2610.41118.method: Near-identical image foils that change one binding (colour, count, relation, state), with many foils per scene.
2610.41118.why: All 22 dual-encoder VLMs score at or below chance, a caution for robots using CLIP-style retrieval to find 'the red one' or 'the one on the left'.

2610.41651.problem: VLM spatial reasoning assumes depth reflects physical distance, which mirrors violate.
2610.41651.method: A real RGB-D dataset from 525 reflective scenes with masks for real and reflected objects, and 14,140 QA pairs from perception to decision-making.
2610.41651.why: Providing depth degraded VLM reasoning, relevant to any indoor robot fusing RGB-D with a VLM near mirrors.

2610.40828.problem: Real-world imitation-learning performance is hard to predict, and validation loss does not track robot success.
2610.40828.method: 281 policies across seven families evaluated in about 1,700 real trials of RJ45 grasping and insertion with a five-fingered hand.
2610.40828.why: Representation choices outweighed optimizer choices, and offline metrics could shortlist but not replace real-robot evaluation.

2610.41130.problem: Accuracy checks on learned world models hide per-test regressions and faults in the test harness itself.
2610.41130.method: Runs each paired video test under four configurations, assigns outcome classes, versions the harness, and compares revisions by per-test transitions.
2610.41130.why: A harness revision that moved accuracy by 2.6 points changed 214 test labels, so compare releases test by test.

2610.41168.problem: LLM performance on ROS code, where correctness only shows once nodes launch and communicate, is largely unmeasured.
2610.41168.method: 108 ROS1-to-ROS2 migration tasks with verified references and runtime test suites exercising topics, services, actions and parameters.
2610.41168.why: pass@1 stays below 10.9% and most failures build cleanly, so LLM-assisted ROS 2 migration needs launch-level tests.

2610.41604.problem: LLM agent systems advertise cognitive modules (theory of mind, global workspace) whose computation may never take effect.
2610.41604.method: A four-question static audit with call-chain tracing plus pre-registered intervention experiments on two systems.
2610.41604.why: In 18 of 25 modules the computed value never reached any output, a reason to audit 'social cognition' components before trusting them in an HRI stack.

2610.41679.problem: Force-augmentation devices are judged on biomechanics on the assumption that perception and decisions follow.
2610.41679.method: An elbow exosuit study measuring weight perception, adaptation in a volatile environment and effort-based decisions with and without assistance.
2610.41679.why: Perception and choices tracked initial experience rather than muscle-load reductions, so human outcomes must be measured directly.

2610.40921.problem: Delivery robots share homes with pets, but navigation is rarely designed with animal welfare in mind.
2610.40921.method: A research-through-design pilot of a curve-out pass at the dog's alert distance, grounded in canine social communication and legible-motion theory.
2610.40921.why: The intended legible manoeuvre caused more stress than a straight pass because it was executed with stops, a reminder that legibility depends on smooth execution.

2610.41724.problem: Robotic partitions, furniture and ceilings reshape spaces people live in, but HRI studies focus on the moment of motion.
2610.41724.method: A reflective essay drawing on the author's previous studies of architectural robots.
2610.41724.why: Argues interaction continues through the configuration left behind and can benefit some occupants while disadvantaging others, relevant to any robot rearranging shared space.

2610.40748.problem: World action models struggle to generalize to tasks outside their video-action training set.
2610.40748.method: Separate video and action experts trained with joint flow matching, plus experiments varying video and action supervision for new tasks.
2610.40748.why: Action-free videos of new tasks more than doubled out-of-distribution success, which suggests where to spend data-collection effort.

2610.41028.problem: Robot-free human demonstrations lose the contact information that dexterous transfer needs.
2610.41028.method: A demonstration interface with shared contact geometry and fingertip views, contact-alignment-first retargeting, and a contact-surface planner in the policy.
2610.41028.why: Gains of at least 50 points in final-stage success on two robot hands, with hardware and software released.

2610.41336.problem: A single human video rarely becomes a dexterous skill that generalizes across placements with natural hand behaviour.
2610.41336.method: Defines the RL objective on object motion and constrains hand-object interaction states toward anatomically natural configurations.
2610.41336.why: Decoupling the skill from the exact hand path is a practical route to reusing one demonstration in new spatial configurations.

2610.42021.problem: Embodiment gaps limit how much egocentric human video contributes to robot action learning.
2610.42021.method: End-to-end human-robot joint training through a hierarchical shared semantic latent used directly for action generation.
2610.42021.why: 80.5% on RoboCasa-GR1 with reported advantages in human-data utilization and real-world generalization.

2610.41127.problem: Vision models learn hand actions only from appearance, without the motor signals behind them.
2610.41127.method: 100 hours of egocentric video paired with bimanual EMG, IMU and audio, used for cross-modal video-EMG pre-training.
2610.41127.why: A motor-grounded representation of human manipulation, useful for recognizing and anticipating what a person's hands are doing.

2610.41334.problem: Open-loop motion generation plus tracking accumulates drift and cannot react to disturbances.
2610.41334.method: Couples a goal-conditioned motion generator with tracking in closed loop, with deviation-decayed recovery, history re-anchoring and latency compensation.
2610.41334.why: Lets a humanoid keep producing plausible motion after pushes and falls instead of replaying a stale reference.

2610.41354.problem: Deterministic humanoid trackers cannot adapt online without brittle reference editing or retraining.
2610.41354.method: A one-step diffusion whole-body controller at 50 Hz, steerable by cost gradients and body-group masks, that flags failures from plan dispersion.
2610.41354.why: Deployed on a Unitree G1, and it identified tracking failures with 91% precision in its top 2% without physics simulation.

2610.41877.problem: Humanoid motion models lack diverse executable data and cannot condition on several modalities in real time.
2610.41877.method: 5 million execution-verified humanoid motions from internet video and one action expert that generates motion from text, speech, music or video with real-time chunking.
2610.41877.why: Speech- and music-conditioned motion is directly relevant to expressive, socially responsive humanoids.

2610.41625.problem: Heavy visual backbones make visuomotor policies too slow for asynchronous closed-loop control on edge hardware.
2610.41625.method: View-aware fusion compresses multi-camera input into a compact token set that conditions a flow-matching action generator.
2610.41625.why: 72.0% success on a real bimanual platform at 32.9 Hz on an RDK S600.

2610.41408.problem: LLM quantization recipes degrade VLAs at ultra-low bit widths.
2610.41408.method: Structure-aware codebook quantization with action-aware mixed-bit allocation and calibration against decoded actions.
2610.41408.why: GR00T N1.7 keeps 93.85% LIBERO success at 1.5 bits with 4.83x less memory, making on-robot VLAs more practical.

2610.41643.problem: Diffusion and flow policies need iterative inference that adds latency and execution mismatch.
2610.41643.method: Directly models clean, observation-conditioned joint-space action chunks for single-step inference, anchored by local 3D geometry and refined for consistency with proprioception.
2610.41643.why: Higher success than two 3D diffusion baselines over 567 trials per method and robustness under repeated 50 N interventions, relevant when people bump the robot.

2610.42097.problem: A humanoid that falls under furniture must make clearance before it can stand.
2610.42097.method: RL with contact-supported geometric escape guidance, a learned motion prior and posture-dependent costs, using proprioception only.
2610.42097.why: 95 of 150 real G1 recoveries across seven obstacle scenes, including furniture arrangements not seen in training.

2610.41654.problem: PPO-based humanoid tracking needs huge sample counts, while first-order methods blow up on contact.
2610.41654.method: Exact simulator gradients with median-relative clipping and multistep regression, on a released differentiable GPU engine for the G1.
2610.41654.why: Reaches a 0.82 tracking score in 20 minutes instead of 1.2 h on one GPU, which shortens iteration on motion skills.

2610.41752.problem: Numerical IK solvers fail near singularities and switch arm aspect unpredictably during tracking.
2610.41752.method: Fourth- and fifth-order solvers with an aspect-preserving step limiter and a certifier with certified restarts.
2610.41752.why: Reported failure reductions of up to four orders of magnitude, released as a C++ library with ROS 2 integration.

2610.41946.problem: Surgical multimodal data collection is costly and tied to particular hardware setups.
2610.41946.method: An open-source Python library for recording, processing, annotating and curating ROS and ROS 2 robot and sensor streams.
2610.41946.why: Evaluated over 1516 recordings; its ROS 2 recording-to-dataset pipeline is reusable outside surgery.

2610.41768.problem: Visual-inertial odometry fails during feature loss and fast motion on wheeled robots.
2610.41768.method: Tightly coupled visual-inertial-encoder RGB-D SLAM with a generative measurement model for wheel encoders.
2610.41768.why: About 2-7 cm RMSE in real time on a differential-drive base, with code and dataset released.

2610.41330.problem: Cross-embodiment navigation policies ignore each robot's geometry and dynamics or need per-robot training.
2610.41330.method: Couples a body-agnostic world model with each robot's differentiable reduced-order ego-dynamics through camera ego-motion.
2610.41330.why: Transfers zero-shot to an unseen real skid-steer robot after three minutes of teleoperated driving for identification.

2610.40799.problem: Small open VLMs fail as code-as-policy agents without frontier models or VLAs.
2610.40799.method: SFT on synthetic trajectories, then multi-turn RL with a physical critic that credits each request using privileged simulator state.
2610.40799.why: A 4B model goes from 0% to 73.8% held-out LIBERO success and runs on a real robot after simulation-only adaptation.

2610.41981.problem: Biological torque controllers for exoskeletons need training data recorded on each new device.
2610.41981.method: An open-source knee exoskeleton whose torque estimator is distilled from a muscle-driven simulation, with no on-device training data.
2610.41981.why: Reduced peak knee extension moment by 21.5% in seven participants; perceptual outcomes were not reported, which 2610.41679 suggests also matter.

2610.41978.problem: Desired endoscope motion depends on the surgeon's intent, which the scene alone does not reveal.
2610.41978.method: Language-conditioned behavioural cloning of six surgeon-requested camera behaviours from 235 subtask demonstrations.
2610.41978.why: One policy that takes short verbal-style requests from a busy human partner, at 100% on three behaviours and 50% on horizon leveling in phantom tests.

2610.41383.problem: Robots executing unfamiliar lab protocols must find missing skills and confirm each step stays valid.
2610.41383.method: Matches requirements to validated skills, requests human teaching for missing ones, and gates progress on precondition, outcome and state checks.
2610.41383.why: 66% and 58% complete-task success on 20- and 31-step dual-arm tasks, a pattern for asking people for help only when needed.

2610.41676.problem: Vessels in narrow canals must coordinate with others without knowing their intentions.
2610.41676.method: Sampling-based MPPI that jointly plans the ego trajectory and predicts the others', with traffic rules encoded as discontinuous costs.
2610.41676.why: No collisions or deadlocks in 780 randomized runs; the joint plan-and-predict pattern carries over to robots moving among people.
